notice: Contains answer keys. Never include in a learner projection, offline package or client bundle.

item.prompt: In an argumentative essay, where does the thesis statement usually appear?
options: At the end of the introduction
In the middle of the second body paragraph
item.hint: Think about what the reader needs to know before the body paragraphs begin.
item.workedExample: The thesis ends the introduction so the reader knows the claim and reasons before the body paragraphs argue them.

item.prompt: Which sentence is an arguable thesis statement?
options: Our school should start a debate club because debating builds confidence and clear thinking.
This essay is about debate clubs.
item.hint: Could a sensible person disagree with it?
item.workedExample: Only the debate-club claim can be argued, and it names two reasons. The others are a fact, an announcement and a topic.

item.prompt: Reason: reading every day builds vocabulary. Which evidence supports this reason best? (Musu's school is the made-up practice school from the lesson.)
options: Musu's class read for 20 minutes a day for one term, and many learners then used new words from the books in their own writing.
item.hint: Which option is specific and proves this exact reason?
item.workedExample: The example from Musu's class is specific and shows vocabulary growing. The others are opinions or unrelated facts. In real writing, the example must come from a real class or a source you can name.

item.prompt: What should the conclusion of an argumentative essay do?
options: Introduce a new reason the reader has not seen
Restate the thesis in new words and sum up the main reasons
Repeat the introduction word for word
item.hint: Remember the three jobs of a conclusion.
item.workedExample: A conclusion restates the thesis in new words, sums up the reasons and ends with a final thought. New reasons belong in the body.

item.prompt: In a PEEL paragraph, what does the Explain sentence do?
options: It shows how the evidence supports the point
It repeats the evidence word for word
item.hint: The Explain sentence answers: so what?
item.workedExample: Explain connects the evidence to the point, showing why the evidence proves it.

options: Some people say a debate club takes time from homework, but meetings can be held once a week after classes.
item.hint: Look for an objection followed by a reply.
item.workedExample: It states an objection (time from homework) and answers it (meet once a week), which is how an essay answers the other side.

writingRubric.use: Formative feedback by the teacher. Not a mastery score; Assessment Player V2 has no constructed-response item type yet.

criteria.label: Thesis statement
criteria.secure: An arguable claim that names two clear reasons.
criteria.developing: A claim with one reason, or reasons that are vague.
criteria.beginning: A topic, a fact or an announcement instead of a claim.

criteria.label: Point (topic sentence)
criteria.secure: States reason one clearly and matches the thesis.
criteria.developing: States a reason that only loosely matches the thesis.
criteria.beginning: No topic sentence, or it repeats the thesis word for word.

criteria.label: Evidence
criteria.secure: Specific, true and relevant evidence (example, checkable fact or experience).
criteria.beginning: Opinion, an invented figure, or unrelated evidence.

criteria.label: Explain and link
criteria.secure: Explains how the evidence proves the point and links back to the claim.
criteria.developing: Explains or links, but not both.
